content.title: Identifying Sampling and Nonresponse Bias
content.overview: This lesson focuses on identifying two critical flaws in survey design: sampling bias (undercoverage) and nonresponse bias. Understanding these concepts allows you to determine if a study's results accurately reflect the target population or if they are skewed by the way participants were selected or how they chose to participate.
learning_objectives: Define and identify sampling bias (undercoverage) in a study design.
Define and identify nonresponse bias based on response rates and respondent demographics.
Apply the Frame-and-Respond Check to evaluate survey validity.
Distinguish between errors in the selection process versus errors in the participation process.

sections.title: Sampling Bias and Undercoverage
sections.content: Sampling bias occurs during the selection phase of a study. It happens when the sampling frame—the actual list or method used to select individuals—does not represent the entire population. The most common form is undercoverage, where specific subgroups of the population have no chance of being selected. For example, if a researcher uses a phone book to select participants, anyone without a listed landline is excluded, creating sampling bias.

sections.title: Nonresponse Bias
sections.content: Nonresponse bias occurs after the sample has been selected. It happens when a significant number of selected individuals do not participate, and those who do respond differ systematically from those who do not. A low response rate (calculated as Respondents ÷ Selected Sample) is a major red flag. If the demographics of the respondents (e.g., gender, age, income) differ significantly from the demographics of the target population, nonresponse bias is likely present.

sections.title: The Frame-and-Respond Check
sections.content:
To evaluate a survey, follow these steps: 1. Identify the Sampling Frame: Who was included in the initial list? If a subgroup was left out, mark 'Sampling Bias.' 2. Calculate the Response Rate: Divide the number of respondents by the number of people contacted. 3. Compare Demographics: Check if the group that actually answered looks like the target population. If the response rate is low and the demographics are skewed, mark 'Nonresponse Bias.' A study can suffer from both biases simultaneously.

![A flowchart showing the steps to identify sampling and nonresponse bias.](https://img.justsolvely.com/followUpImage/1f792355-4bbe-4090-bb03-e181930349f0-1786506150745-994.webp)

worked_examples.question: A city council wants to gauge interest in a new park. They mail surveys to 5,000 households listed in the property tax database. The city also contains 1,500 apartment-dwelling households who do not pay property taxes directly and were not mailed surveys. Of the 5,000 mailed, 400 were returned. The respondents were 80% homeowners, while the city overall is 60% homeowners. Identify the biases present.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Check the sampling frame. The property tax database was used, which excluded 1,500 apartment-dwelling households. Because a subgroup was excluded from the selection process, Sampling Bias (undercoverage) is present. Step 2: Calculate the response rate. 400 respondents / 5,000 selected = 8%. This is a very low response rate. Step 3: Compare demographics. The respondents are 80% homeowners, but the city is only 60% homeowners. The people who chose to respond differ significantly from the population. Therefore, Nonresponse Bias is also present. Conclusion: Both sampling bias and nonresponse bias are present.

common_mistakes: Confusing sampling bias with nonresponse bias: Remember that sampling bias is about who *could* be picked, while nonresponse bias is about who *chose* to answer.
Ignoring the denominator: When calculating response rates, always divide by the number of people contacted, not the total population.
Assuming a large sample size fixes bias: A large sample that is biased (e.g., only surveying people at a luxury mall) will still produce incorrect results regardless of how many people are asked.
exam_tips: If the problem mentions a specific group was 'left out' or 'not contacted,' look for sampling bias.
If the problem provides a low percentage of returned surveys or mentions that respondents have different traits than the general population, look for nonresponse bias.
Watch for 'Voluntary Response' as a distractor; while related, ACT questions often specifically ask you to identify undercoverage or nonresponse based on the provided data.
content.recap: Sampling bias (undercoverage) occurs when the selection method excludes parts of the population. Nonresponse bias occurs when the people who fail to respond differ from those who do. Use the Frame-and-Respond Check to identify if one, both, or neither bias affects a study's results.

knowledge_claims.content: Sampling bias occurs when the method used to select a sample results in a sample that is not representative of the population.
Undercoverage is a specific type of sampling bias that occurs when some members of the population are inadequately represented in the sampling frame.
The sampling frame is the actual list or set of procedures from which a sample is drawn.
Nonresponse bias occurs when individuals chosen for a sample are unable or unwilling to participate, and these individuals differ systematically from those who do participate.
The response rate is calculated by dividing the number of respondents by the total number of individuals selected for the sample.
A low response rate (often below 20%) is a primary indicator that nonresponse bias may be affecting the survey results.
Sampling bias happens during the selection phase (before participation), whereas nonresponse bias happens during the participation phase (after selection).
To identify sampling bias, check if any specific subgroups of the target population were excluded from the initial sampling frame.
To identify nonresponse bias, compare the demographic characteristics of the respondents to the demographic characteristics of the target population.
If a survey excludes a subgroup from the frame AND has a low response rate with skewed demographics, both sampling bias and nonresponse bias are present.
It is a mistake to assume that a large number of respondents eliminates bias if the sampling frame itself was flawed.
A survey is considered valid only if the sampling frame includes the entire population and the respondents represent a high, unbiased percentage of that frame.

items.stem:
Practice form 1.
Which survey design is most clearly biased?

options.A: Ask only gym members whether the city should build more gyms.
options.C: Use a complete resident list for selection.
options.D: Allow selected residents to answer anonymously.

items.explanation: Sampling only gym members overrepresents a group with a strong interest.

videoLesson.title: Identify Sampling and Nonresponse Bias
videoLesson.description: You will recognize excluded groups and skewed respondent data in survey results. Check the sampling frame and response rates to decide if undercoverage or biased nonresponse explains differences.
